# Transformers and Attention {#sec-transformers}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**Chapter status: core sections drafted, later sections in outline.** The two
interactive explorers below are fully functional.
:::

**Learning objectives.** After this chapter you can:

- explain self-attention as a *learned weighted average* over token representations;
- read the equation $\operatorname{Attention}(Q,K,V)=\operatorname{softmax}\!\big(QK^{\top}/\sqrt{d_k}\big)\,V$ term by term;
- describe why multiple heads exist and what different heads specialize in;
- explain how a model turns scores into text — and what temperature, top-k, and top-p actually do to the distribution.

## The problem attention solves

By @sec-language-models we could predict the next word, but our recurrent
models had a bottleneck: everything the model knew about the sentence had to
be squeezed through a fixed-size state, one step at a time. Long-range
relationships — a pronoun and the noun it refers to, a verb and its distant
subject — kept getting lost.

The Transformer's answer [@vaswani2017attention] is almost embarrassingly
direct: [let every token look at every other token, and learn how much each
one matters]{.hl}. If you have ever computed a weighted average, you already
own the core intuition. Attention is a weighted average of token vectors
where *the weights themselves are predicted from the data*.

## Self-attention, step by step

Each token's vector is projected three ways — a **query** ("what am I looking
for?"), a **key** ("what do I contain?"), and a **value** ("what do I pass
along if selected?"). The score between token $i$ and token $j$ is the dot
product $q_i \cdot k_j$, scaled and pushed through a softmax so each row
becomes a probability distribution:

$$
\operatorname{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \operatorname{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right) V
$$

That softmax row is exactly the set of weights in the weighted average. A
statistician's translation: for every token, the model runs a tiny,
data-dependent regression over the whole sentence deciding *which other
tokens are informative right now*.

### Explore: what is a head looking at?

Different attention heads learn different, often interpretable, habits. The
widget below shows a stylized attention matrix for one sentence. Each **row**
is a token doing the looking; each **column** is a token being looked at;
darker means more weight. Switch heads and watch the pattern change —
especially the row for `it`.

::: {.anlp-widget}
```{=html}
<div class="widget-title">Attention head explorer — “The robot poured coffee because it was ready.”</div>
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof headChoice = Inputs.radio(
  [
    "Pronoun head — what does “it” attend to?",
    "Previous-token head",
    "Uniform head (bag of words)"
  ],
  { value: "Pronoun head — what does “it” attend to?", label: "" }
)
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
attnData = {
  const tokens = ["The", "robot", "poured", "coffee", "because", "it", "was", "ready", "."];
  const n = tokens.length;
  const M = Array.from({ length: n }, () => new Array(n).fill(0));

  if (headChoice.startsWith("Previous")) {
    for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
      if (i === 0) { M[i][i] = 1; }
      else { M[i][i - 1] = 0.82; M[i][i] = 0.18; }
    }
  } else if (headChoice.startsWith("Uniform")) {
    for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) for (let j = 0; j < n; j++) M[i][j] = 1 / n;
  } else {
    // Pronoun (coreference-flavored) head
    for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) { M[i][i] = 0.62; if (i > 0) M[i][i - 1] = 0.38; }
    const it = tokens.indexOf("it");
    M[it] = new Array(n).fill(0);
    M[it][tokens.indexOf("robot")]  = 0.46;  // is “it” the robot…
    M[it][tokens.indexOf("coffee")] = 0.34;  // …or the coffee?
    M[it][it] = 0.12;
    M[it][tokens.indexOf("ready")]  = 0.08;
  }

  const cells = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < n; i++)
    for (let j = 0; j < n; j++)
      cells.push({ from: tokens[i], to: tokens[j], w: M[i][j] });
  return { tokens, cells };
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
Plot.plot({
  width: 640,
  height: 480,
  marginLeft: 70,
  marginBottom: 60,
  x: { domain: attnData.tokens, label: "…attends to (key)", tickRotate: -35 },
  y: { domain: [...attnData.tokens].reverse(), label: "token (query)…" },
  color: { type: "linear", range: ["#F2F5F5", "#0E7C7B"], label: "attention weight", legend: true },
  marks: [
    Plot.cell(attnData.cells, {
      x: "to", y: "from", fill: "w", inset: 1.5, rx: 4,
      title: d => `${d.from} → ${d.to}: ${d.w.toFixed(2)}`
    })
  ]
})
```

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" icon="false"}
The ambiguity in the pronoun head is real, and it is the classic
*Winograd* setup: in "…because it was **ready**", `it` is probably the
coffee; swap in "…because it was **empty**" and `it` flips to the pot.
Resolving that takes world knowledge — which is exactly what large-scale
pretraining buys.
:::
:::

## Multi-head attention, positions, and the block

<!-- TODO(draft): why h parallel heads; concatenation + output projection;
     positional information (learned vs RoPE); residual + layer norm; the
     full Transformer block diagram. Port figures from the CME 295-based
     workshop deck. -->

One head is one habit; real models run dozens in parallel and mix the
results. Because attention itself is order-blind, position must be injected
explicitly — the model literally cannot tell "dog bites man" from "man bites
dog" without it.

## From scores to text: decoding

A language model's forward pass ends in a vector of **logits** — one raw
score per vocabulary token. What happens next is not learning; it is a
[sampling policy you control at inference time]{.hl}, and it changes the
character of the output more than most people expect.

- **Temperature** $\tau$ rescales logits before the softmax:
  $p_i \propto \exp(z_i/\tau)$. Low $\tau$ sharpens, high $\tau$ flattens.
- **Top-k** keeps only the $k$ highest-probability tokens, then renormalizes.
- **Top-p (nucleus)** keeps the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative
  probability exceeds $p$, then renormalizes [@holtzman2020curious].

### Explore: temperature, top-k, and top-p

The model has just read *"After the lecture, the students were completely
____"* and produced the logits below. Gray bars show the raw softmax
distribution; teal bars show what survives your sampling policy, after
renormalization. Try $\tau = 0.2$, then $\tau = 1.8$. Then cut the tail with
top-p $= 0.6$.

::: {.anlp-widget}
```{=html}
<div class="widget-title">Sampling policy explorer — the same logits, reshaped</div>
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof temperature = Inputs.range([0.1, 2.0], { value: 1.0, step: 0.05, label: "Temperature τ" })
```
```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof topK = Inputs.range([1, 12], { value: 12, step: 1, label: "Top-k" })
```
```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof topP = Inputs.range([0.05, 1.0], { value: 1.0, step: 0.05, label: "Top-p (nucleus)" })
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
samplingDist = {
  const candidates = [
    { token: "exhausted",   logit:  4.2 },
    { token: "confused",    logit:  3.7 },
    { token: "silent",      logit:  3.1 },
    { token: "inspired",    logit:  2.9 },
    { token: "lost",        logit:  2.5 },
    { token: "quiet",       logit:  2.2 },
    { token: "bored",       logit:  1.8 },
    { token: "energized",   logit:  1.4 },
    { token: "hungry",      logit:  1.0 },
    { token: "transformed", logit:  0.5 },
    { token: "purple",      logit: -0.5 },
    { token: "recursive",   logit: -1.2 }
  ];

  // 1) temperature-scaled softmax
  const ws = candidates.map(d => Math.exp(d.logit / temperature));
  const Z = ws.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
  let rows = candidates
    .map((d, i) => ({ ...d, p: ws[i] / Z }))
    .sort((a, b) => b.p - a.p);

  // 2) top-k filter
  rows = rows.map((d, i) => ({ ...d, kept: i < topK }));

  // 3) top-p (nucleus) filter over what survived top-k
  let cum = 0;
  rows = rows.map(d => {
    const before = cum;
    if (d.kept) cum += d.p;
    return { ...d, kept: d.kept && before < topP };
  });

  // 4) renormalize the survivors
  const Zk = rows.filter(d => d.kept).reduce((a, d) => a + d.p, 0) || 1;
  return rows.map(d => ({ ...d, pFinal: d.kept ? d.p / Zk : 0 }));
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
Plot.plot({
  width: 640,
  height: 380,
  marginLeft: 100,
  x: {
    label: "P(next token)",
    domain: [0, Math.max(0.4, ...samplingDist.map(d => d.pFinal), ...samplingDist.map(d => d.p)) * 1.15],
    tickFormat: ".0%"
  },
  y: { domain: samplingDist.map(d => d.token), label: null },
  marks: [
    Plot.barX(samplingDist, { y: "token", x: "p", fill: "#D4DADF" }),
    Plot.barX(samplingDist.filter(d => d.kept), { y: "token", x: "pFinal", fill: "#0E7C7B" }),
    Plot.text(samplingDist.filter(d => d.kept), {
      y: "token", x: "pFinal",
      text: d => (d.pFinal * 100).toFixed(1) + "%",
      dx: 6, textAnchor: "start", fill: "#5B6272", fontSize: 11
    }),
    Plot.ruleX([0])
  ]
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
md`**${samplingDist.filter(d => d.kept).length} of 12** candidate tokens survive
this policy. Gray = raw softmax at τ = ${temperature.toFixed(2)}; teal =
renormalized sampling distribution.`
```
:::

Notice what a low temperature does *not* do: it never changes the ranking,
only the contrast. Top-k and top-p, by comparison, are hard cutoffs — they
exist mainly to stop the model from ever picking `recursive` in a sentence
about tired students. This trio is your first, cheapest lever in every
applied system you will build in Part III.

## Where to go deeper

Three outside visualizations pair beautifully with this chapter: the
[Illustrated Transformer](https://jalammar.github.io/illustrated-transformer/)
for step-by-step diagrams, Georgia Tech's
[Transformer Explainer](https://poloclub.github.io/transformer-explainer/),
which runs a live GPT-2 in your browser, and Brendan Bycroft's
[3D LLM walkthrough](https://bbycroft.net/llm).

## Exercises

1. In the attention explorer, the pronoun head splits its weight roughly
   46/34 between *robot* and *coffee*. Rewrite the sentence so a good model
   should flip that ratio, and justify your edit.
2. Show algebraically that temperature scaling never changes the argmax
   token. What does this imply about greedy decoding?
3. Set $\tau = 1$, top-k $= 12$. Find the smallest top-p that still keeps
   at least four tokens. Explain the cumulative-mass logic behind your
   answer.
